senses.def: the elder brother of Moses and Israel’s first high priest
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἄγριος ‘wild, savage’) pertaining to what is violent and uncontrolled
senses.comment: This expression in Jude 1:13, however, is applied to people, and therefore it may be necessary to make the figurative reference clear, for example, they are like stormy waves of the sea or … wild waves of the sea.

senses.def: pertaining to what is undomesticated and uncultivated in nature

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: red liquid that circulates in the arteries and veins of humans and animals
senses.comment: In Mark 5:25 it may be important to use a special term for blood, since this passage is a reference to the hemorrhaging of menstruation.|In John 19:34 (ἐξῆλθεν εὐθὺς αἷμα καὶ ὕδωρ ‘then blood and water came out’) it may be necessary to use a term which can refer to the lymph fluid rather than to water itself; otherwise the reader might understand the water as being urine (with the spear having pierced the bladder) or even possibly water that Jesus had presumably drunk and was still in his stomach. The real reference of ὕδωρ in John 19:34 is to the lymph fluid and not to water as such. It is simply a colorless fluid which was mixed with blood.|In Revelation 8:8 (καὶ ἐγένετο τὸ τρίτον τῆς θαλάσσης αἷμα ‘and a third of the sea became blood’) and Revelation 11:6 (καὶ ἐξουσίαν ἔχουσιν ἐπὶ τῶν ὑδάτων στρέφειν αὐτὰ εἰς αἷμα ‘and they had power over the waters to turn them into blood’) the reference may not be to blood as a substance but to the blood-like color of the objects in question.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of αἷμα[a] ‘blood,’ 8.64) the death of a person, generally as the result of violence or execution
senses.comment: It is possible to interpret αἷμα in Romans 5:9 (δικαιωθέντες νῦν ἐν τῷ αἵματι αὐτοῦ ‘by his death we are put right with God’) as primarily a reference to physiological death. But in such contexts in which αἷμα is used in speaking of the death of Christ, there is no doubt an additional component derived from the occurrence of αἷμα in contexts speaking of atoning sacrifice. Therefore, one may analyze the meaning of αἷμα in such contexts as meaning ‘sacrificial death’ and not merely physiological death. In Romans 5:9 and similar contexts, a number of translators have preferred to preserve an often recurring phrase such as ‘the shedding of his blood.’ However, in English this can be somewhat ambiguous in that ‘the shedding of blood’ normally refers to the killing of someone else and not to experiencing death. See also 23.112.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of αἷμα[a] ‘blood,’ 8.64) to deprive a person of life by violent means
(an idiom, literally: to pour out blood) to cause the death of someone by violent means
senses.comment: The phrase πᾶν αἷμα δίκαιον ἐκχυννόμενον in Matthew 23:35 may be literally translated as ‘all innocent blood that is poured out.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: the blood pours out) to die, with the implication of a sacrificial purpose
senses.comment: The relations between the various elements in this clause in Matthew 26:28 must in some instances be made somewhat more specific, for example, ‘by my dying, I am like a sacrifice for many for the purpose of their sins being forgiven.’ See also 23.107.

senses.def: (set phrases, literally: fountain of blood, and: flow of blood, respectively) the loss of blood through menstrual bleeding
(an idiom, literally: flesh and blood) a human being in contrast with a divine being
(an idiom, literally: to share blood and flesh) to have the characteristics and nature of a human being
to acquire information in an exact and accurate manner or to acquire information which is exact and accurate

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time which is emphatically simultaneous with another point of time
a marker of association, involving additional items affected by some event
to read something written, normally done aloud and thus involving verbalization
senses.comment: In areas where literacy is a relatively new factor in the culture, idiomatic expressions are often employed for reading, for example, ‘to let paper speak’ or ‘to mouth the marks on paper’ or ‘to see speech.’

senses.def: to cause someone distress and worry
pertaining to not being washed
to consider something of a comparable merit or worth
glosses: to regard as being valuable for
senses.comment: It is possible that in Luke 7:7 the focus is upon social status, and in many languages the equivalent would be ‘I do not think of myself as being important enough to come to you.’ In some languages the idea of ‘not being important enough’ may be rendered figuratively as ‘being too small a person.’

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to make a choice on the basis of greater worth
to desire something on the basis of its evident worth or value
the event of registering persons in connection with taking a census
senses.comment: One may construct a descriptive equivalent of ‘census’ by speaking of ‘when everyone’s name is taken down and he is counted’ or ‘a time when the government writes down everyone’s name on a list’ or ‘… in books.’

senses.def: to take the roof off of a house
senses.comment: In Mark 2:4 ἀποστεγάζω refers to only a part of the roof, and therefore in a number of languages it may be necessary to translate as ‘they made a hole in the roof.’ In view of the type of houses built in Palestine in NT times, the roof no doubt would have been flat, held up by heavy beams over which were laid planks or sticks and then covered with sun-baked clay.

senses.def: a person whose family is greeted in the Epistle to the Romans
(derivative of Ἀσία ‘Asia,’ 93.415) a person who is a native of Asia
to grow, to increase in size, whether of animate beings or of plants
senses.comment: In a number of languages one must make a clear distinction in the choice of terms referring to the growth of an animate being (animal or human) and the growth of plants|In Colossians 2:19 αὔξησις is used figuratively in the sense that the reference of ‘body’ is the church rather than a physical body. Normally a term for ‘growth’ would imply not only size but also number, that is to say, the growth of the church would be in terms of the increase of members of the church, though it might refer to spiritual maturity. In some instances, however, it may be necessary to specify ‘growth in numbers’ so as to avoid the implication which might be derived from the context, namely, that the church is simply a building which gets bigger and bigger.

senses.def: the distance beneath a surface
senses.comment: In some languages it may be best to say ‘because there was not much soil’ Matthew 13:5.

senses.def: a place that is deep
an extreme point on a scale of extent

senses.subdomain: Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
senses.def: a place or region which is low
senses.comment: As in the case of ὕψωμα[a] (1.13), βάθος may be interpreted as a supernatural force ([e]).|The phrase κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς ‘the lower parts of the earth’ may likewise refer to ‘the world below’ as in εἰς τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς ‘down into the lower parts of the earth’ Romans 8:39 (see 83.54). Some scholars, however, understand this expression as being a reference to the earth which is low in contrast with heaven. On the basis of such an interpretation one may render Romans 8:39 as ‘he came down to the earth itself.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of βάθος[a] ‘depth,’ 81.8) supernatural powers in the region below the earth
senses.comment: See 12.46 for an illustrative passage in Romans 8:38. For another interpretation of βάθος in Romans 8:39, see βάθος[d] 1.18.|As in the case of ὕψωμα[b] (12.46), βάθος[e] has been interpreted by some as indicating merely the distance which a person might be separated from God, but most scholars assume that the reference here is to ‘the powers of the world below.’

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of βάθος[a] ‘depth,’ 81.8) the content of knowledge which is very difficult to know
glosses: secrets difficult to find out about
senses.comment: Only rarely can one use a literal rendering of τὰ βαθέα or τὰ βάθη in referring to secrets. In some instances it may be possible to use an expression such as ‘far away’ or ‘distant,’ and in other cases one can use expressions meaning ‘hard’ or ‘difficult.’ More often than not, however, the closest equivalent of τὰ βαθέα and τὰ βάθη in this type of context is either an expression of degree using a term such as ‘very’ (for example, ‘that which is very secret’) or an expression implying ‘that which is hidden’ or ‘that which is difficult to discover.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: (derivative of βραδύς ‘slow,’ 67.123) to extend a period of time, with the implication of slowness and/or delay
coming into existence by birth
senses.comment: In some languages ‘from the time he was born’ may be best rendered as ‘from the time he was a small baby.’ One may also render this expression of time as ‘a man who had always been blind’ or ‘a man who had never been able to see.’

senses.def: an evil supernatural being or spirit
senses.comment: While in a number of languages the Devil may be spoken of as ‘the chief of the demons,’ sometimes the demons are simply called ‘the spirits of the Devil’ or ‘the servants of the Devil.’|In a number of languages the difficulty in terminology for demons is not the absence of a term, but the abundance of different terms for different kinds of demons, each one of which may be responsible for particular kinds of human behavior, for example, insanity, depression, epilepsy, sex perversion, and violent assault. Sometimes demons are classified as ‘those of the home’ and ‘those of the forest,’ in which case the latter are normally regarded as more violent and virulent. When there is an abundance of different terms for demons and no generic term for all types of demons, one can usually select a class of demons which parallels most closely the descriptions of demon activity in the NT and use such a term with appropriate contextual qualifications so as to suggest that such a term is to be understood in a general sense.

senses.def: a supernatural being of somewhat lesser status than θεός[b] ‘god’ (12.22)
senses.comment: The expression ‘foreign gods’ (Acts 17:18) may be rendered as ‘gods whom the foreigners worshiped’ or ‘gods of the foreigners.’ It would be wrong to render ‘foreign gods’ by a phrase which would mean ‘the gods are foreigners.’

senses.def: one who holds complete power or authority over another
glosses: Lord (as a title for God and for Christ)

senses.def: one who owns and/or controls the activities of slaves, servants, or subjects, with the implication of absolute, and in some instances, arbitrary jurisdiction
to be divided into opposing and hostile units
to complete movement in a particular direction
senses.comment: It would also be possible to translate διέρχομαι in Acts 11:19 as ‘arrived’ or ‘finally reached.’

senses.def: to travel around through an area, with the implication of both extensive and thorough movement throughout an area
senses.comment: In order to express the meaning of διοδεύω, διαπορεύομαι[a], and διέρχομαι[b] in these types of contexts, it may be necessary in some languages to say ‘he went from one town to another’ or, as in Acts 13:6, ‘he travelled to all the places on the island’ or ‘… to the various towns on the island.’

senses.subdomain: Pass, Cross Over, Go Through, Go Around
senses.def: to move from one side to another of some geographical object (for example, body of water, chasm, valley, etc.)

senses.subdomain: Pass, Cross Over, Go Through, Go Around
senses.def: to move through a three-dimensional space
senses.comment: The use of διέρχομαι in Acts 12:10 would suggest that the guard station was some kind of enclosure where guards stayed to control passage.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: a sword goes through one’s soul) to feel the intense pain of sorrow
a position relatively close to another position

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time subsequent to another point of time, but relatively close
to move into a space, either two-dimensional or three-dimensional
to become so tired and weary as to give out (possibly even to faint from exhaustion)
senses.comment: A number of languages make a clear distinction between (1) fainting as the result of surprise, astonishment, or fear and (2) fainting from physical exhaustion.

senses.def: to lose one’s motivation to accomplish some valid goal

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being deserving of pity in view of one’s miserable condition
(derivative of ἐμφανίζω[a] ‘to make visible,’ 24.19) pertaining to that which has been made visible
pertaining to not having been known before but having become evident
to prepare a body for burial
to demand that a person take an oath as to the truth of what is said or as to the certainty that one will carry out the request or command
glosses: to insist that one take an oath
senses.comment: It is extremely difficult to translate ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω in a literal manner, though in some contexts one can say ‘I put you under oath,’ but in a number of passages the person speaking is imploring and not necessarily in a position to command or insist. Therefore, in a passage such as Mark 5:7, one may render the meaning idiomatically as ‘for God’s sake, I ask you, do not punish me.’ In 1 Thessalonians 5:27 one may translate ‘in the name of the Lord, I ask you to read this letter to all the Christian brothers,’ and in Matthew 26:63 one may translate ‘in the name of the living God, I charge you, Tell us who you are.’|In most languages one may translate ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω by simply adding a causative component to terms meaning ‘to swear’ or ‘to take an oath.’ In other words, ὁρκίζω, ἐνορκίζω, and ἐξορκίζω may be rendered as ‘to cause a person to say under oath.’

senses.def: to ask for information
senses.comment: In a number of languages a term such as ἐρωτάω[a] or ἐπερωτάω[a] implies an introduction of direct discourse, so that in Luke 9:45, for example, it may be necessary to translate ‘they were afraid to ask him, What do you mean by what you said?’

senses.def: to ask for, usually with the implication of an underlying question
to attempt in a legal or semi-legal procedure to know the truth about a matter, normally by interrogation
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἐπιπλήσσω ‘to strike,’ not occurring in the NT) to express strong disapproval as a type of punishment
(derivative of οὐρανός[a] ‘sky,’ 1.5) related to or located in the sky
senses.comment: For ἐπουράνιος as part of an idiom, see 1.26.

senses.def: (derivative of οὐρανός[b] heaven, 1.11) related to or located in heaven
senses.comment: The derivatives οὐράνιος and ἐπουράνιος[b] are essentially equivalent to semantic compounds in that they combine a semantic element of heaven as a celestial abode with another semantic element specifying location or relationship. Frequently such terms are translated as ‘in heaven’ or ‘from heaven’ or ‘belonging to heaven.’

senses.def: (derivative of οὐρανός[c] ‘God,’ 12.16) pertaining to being derived from God
senses.comment: Though it is possible to interpret Hebrews 3:1 as a ‘calling which comes from heaven,’ it seems more appropriate in terms of the frequent references to ‘calling’ to recognize that the use of ἐπουράνιος in this context is simply a substitute for a direct reference to God. Accordingly, the passage may be effectively rendered as ‘those who have been called by God’ or ‘those whom God has called.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: heavenly body, occurring in the NT only in the plural) the luminous objects in the sky: sun, moon, and other planets and stars
senses.comment: See also 1.8.|The phrase σῶμα ἐπουράνιον is a highly generic expression which in the plural is sometimes translatable as ‘lights in the sky,’ but more often than not it may be necessary to identify the various heavenly bodies as ‘sun, moon, and stars.’ In certain contexts one may also wish to identify the planets, often spoken of as ‘wandering stars’ or ‘moving stars’ (reflecting the etymology of the English word planet, which is derived from a Greek word meaning ‘wanderer’). These are, of course, not to be confused with shooting stars and comets in the sky.

senses.def: pertaining to events which measure up to their intended purpose
senses.comment: In the 65.23 contexts, βελτίων, καλῶς[b], εὖ[b], and εὖγε occur in highly elliptical constructions.

senses.def: to cause someone to be or become happy or glad
to rejoice as an expression of happiness
senses.comment: In some languages it may be necessary to translate εὐφραίνομαι in Acts 2:26 in an idiomatic manner, for example, ‘my heart sings’ or ‘my heart shouts because it is happy.’ For another interpretation of εὐφραίνομαι in Acts 7:41, see 51.3.

senses.def: to celebrate an occasion, with the implication of happiness and joy
senses.comment: For another interpretation of εὐφραίνομαι in Acts 7:41, see 25.122.

senses.def: (derivative of ἡγεμών[a] ‘ruler,’ 37.59) to be a governor, in the NT restricted to the meaning of a governor of a Roman province
senses.comment: The expression ‘Quirinius was governor of Syria’ (Luke 2:2) may be rendered in some languages as ‘Quirinius was the one who commanded all those in the province of Syria’ or ‘Quirinius gave orders to all those in Syria.’

senses.def: to observe something with continuity and attention, often with the implication that what is observed is something unusual
to go to see a person on the basis of friendship and with helpful intent
a city in Lydia
pertaining to being cheerfully happy
an OT prophet

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being bad, with the implication of harmful and damaging
pertaining to being harsh and difficult
senses.comment: In a number of languages one cannot speak of ‘experiencing bad things’; rather, one must say in Luke 16:25 ‘suffered a great deal’ or ‘always lived with difficulty’ or ‘always had troubles.’

senses.def: pertaining to having experienced harm
senses.comment: In some languages Acts 28:5 may be rendered as ‘but Paul shook the snake off into the fire, and it did not cause him pain at all.’

senses.def: pertaining to being incorrect or inaccurate, with the possible implication of also being reprehensible
that which has been cursed
(derivative of κατασκήνωσις ‘nest,’ 6.146) to make a nest (or possibly to find shelter)
heat sufficiently intense to cause suffering or burning
senses.comment: In some languages the effect of heat may be described simply as ‘heat will not scorch them’ or ‘they will not suffer because of heat.’ Such expressions, however, may be ambiguous because they might mean that the individuals involved would be able to easily withstand the heat. The meaning of the biblical passage, however, is that there would be no heat to cause them harm.

senses.def: Tiberius Claudius Nero Germanicus (compare 93.359), a Roman emperor, who ruled from 41 A.D. to 54 A.D.
Claudius Lysias, a Roman officer in Jerusalem
dust, soil (see also 2.16)
senses.comment: ‘Shake the dust from your feet’ may be expressed as ‘kick the dust from your feet.’ In some instances, however, the more appropriate equivalent would be ‘get rid of the dust from your feet’ or even ‘remove the dust from your feet and leave it there.’

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: pertaining to being secret as a result of people not knowing
a city in Phrygia in Asia Minor
to argue or quarrel about the meaning or use of words
a position at a relatively great distance from another position

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to become drunk on alcoholic beverages
to drink wine or beer (distilled alcoholic beverages were not known in the ancient world), usually with emphasis upon drinking relatively large quantities
to be very concerned about, with the implication of placing too much value upon something
pertaining to being almost mute
senses.comment: In translating μογιλάλος it may be necessary in some instances to use a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘when he spoke, people could hardly understand’ or ‘he spoke in such a way that people had difficulty in understanding.’

senses.def: to experience or suffer shipwreck
senses.comment: In some languages it is necessary to specify the particular cause of a shipwreck, for example, ‘the ship struck a rock or reef’ or ‘the ship sank because of a storm’ or ‘the ship collided with another ship and sank.’ In view of the context of 2 Corinthians 11:25, it is probably best to select an expression which would refer to a ship sinking because of a storm, though obviously one cannot be certain.

senses.def: a collective for the young of birds hatched in a nest
to make or erect any kind of construction
to increase the potential of someone or something, with focus upon the process involved
to speak disparagingly of a person in a manner which is not justified
to reproach someone, with the implication of that individual being evidently to blame

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being holy in the sense of superior moral qualities and possessing certain essentially divine qualities in contrast with what is human
(derivative of παιδεύω[a] ‘to train,’ 33.226) one who provides instruction for the purpose of proper behavior
(derivative of παιδεύω[c] ‘to punish,’ 38.4) a person who punishes for constructive purposes
to refuse to listen to and hence to disobey
senses.comment: It would be a mistake to translate παρακούω[a], παρακοή, and παραιτέομαι[e] as meaning nothing more than ‘not to listen to.’ The meaning is clearly ‘to refuse to listen to’ or ‘to refuse to pay attention to,’ and hence ‘to disobey.’ It may therefore be best in a number of instances to translate ‘to refuse to obey.’

senses.def: to hear something without the speakers knowledge or intent
senses.comment: Some scholars understand παρακούω in Mark 5:36 as meaning ‘to ignore’ or ‘to overlook’ (see 30.37).

senses.def: to not pay attention to something
senses.comment: Some scholars understand παρακούω in Mark 5:36 as meaning ‘to overhear’ (see 24.66).

senses.def: (derivative of παροικέω[b] ‘to sojourn,’ 85.78) the time or occasion of one’s living in a place as a foreigner
fifteenth in a series involving time, space, or set
an area or region around or near some central or focal point
senses.comment: In certain contexts, however, περίχωρος may include not only the surrounding region but also the point of reference, for example, τῆς περιχώρου τῶν Γερασηνῶν ‘the Gerasenes and the people living around them’ Luke 8:37. In a context such as Matthew 3:5, ἡ περίχωρος τοῦ Ἰορδάνου, it is difficult to speak of ‘the area surrounding the Jordan River,’ since a river is not like a city which would constitute a center. Accordingly, one must often translate ἡ περίχωρος τοῦ Ἰορδάνου as ‘the land on both sides of the River Jordan.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a person who is pugnacious and demanding
a region in northeast Asia Minor
(derivative of πρόβατον ‘sheep,’ 4.22) pertaining to sheep
senses.comment: The phrase ἐπὶ τῇ προβατικῇ is an elliptical expression in which the noun for ‘gate’ (which is feminine in gender) is omitted. The phrase ‘at the Sheep Gate’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘close to the gate of the city through which sheep entered’ or ‘… were driven’ or ‘… were led.’

senses.def: to add to or to extend one’s threats
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand προσαπειλέομαι in Acts 4:21 as meaning ‘to threaten besides.’

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: pertaining to a point of time earlier in a sequence
first, with the implication of emphasis, frequently in reference to time
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand πρότερος in Galatians 4:13 as meaning ‘earlier, formerly’ (see 67.18).

senses.def: a companion of Paul
the capital city of the Roman Empire

a celestial body smaller than the sun that gives light to earth in the nighttime; the moon’s appearance changes over the course of each month as the angle we can see the moon’s half-illuminated surface changes
senses.comment: As in the case of ἥλιος the sun (1.28), there are relatively few difficulties involved in obtaining a satisfactory word for σελήνη ‘the moon,’ though there may also be a tendency to add some kind of honorific or title, for example, ‘mother moon.’ At the same time, certain difficulties may occur in some passages. For example, in Luke 21:25 it may be misleading to speak of signs occurring ‘in the moon,’ for this might mean ‘inside the moon.’ TEV has resolved the problem somewhat by translating “there will be strange things happening to the sun, the moon, and the stars.” One may also translate ‘the sun, the moon, and the stars will cause signs in the heavens’ or ‘… portents in the sky.’

senses.def: pertaining to being harsh and violent
senses.comment: For another interpretation of σκληρός in James 3:4, see 76.15.

senses.def: pertaining to being powerful or strong
senses.comment: For another interpretation of σκληρός in James 3:4, see 20.3.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being harsh or possibly cruel in one’s behavior
senses.comment: In a number of languages σκληρός in Jude 1:15 may be translated as ‘words that cause pain’ or idiomatically as ‘words that are like daggers.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being hard and demanding in one’s behavior
a basket which is presumably somewhat larger than a κόφινος (6.150)
a reference to a receptor of a message (with an added feature of emphasis in the form σύ)
a reference to the receptors of a message, whether oral or written (with an added feature of emphasis in the form ὑμεῖς)
to suffer along with someone else
glosses: to share in the sufferings of
senses.comment: It is, however, possible to interpret συμπαθέω in Hebrews 10:34 as referring primarily to sympathy rather than actual sharing or suffering.

senses.def: to share someone’s feeling in the sense of being sympathetic with
senses.comment: In a number of languages the closest equivalent of ‘being sympathetic with’ may be ‘to understand completely how one feels’ or ‘to feel in one’s heart just like someone else feels.’

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: pertaining to being selected together with
senses.comment: As indicated in some of the renderings of terms expressing choice and selection, it is often preferable, and frequently necessary, to indicate who does the choosing. Therefore, it is often advisable or necessary to indicate the agent, whether in an active or passive construction.

senses.def: to cause to come together, whether of animate or inanimate objects
the movement of two or more objects to the same location
senses.comment: In a number of languages important distinctions are made in terms referring to gathering or assembling of animate beings. The distinctions are usually based upon the number of individuals, the distance which they have come, and whether or not the individuals in question constitute a membership group or whether they are merely a loose aggregation. In view of these types of distinctions, it is likely that quite different terms will be required for the various contexts listed for this set of related meanings.

senses.def: a construction for the burial of the dead; often a natural cave or hewn out of bedrock
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is important to distinguish clearly between a grave (a hole in the ground in which a corpse is placed) and a tomb (a construction built above the surface of the ground for housing a corpse). In some contexts, however, it may be better to use a more generic expression, for example, ‘places where people are buried’ or ‘places where corpses are placed.’ In Mark 5:2 it is important to avoid a term which would designate merely graves, for the demoniac who met Jesus was not living down in graves in the ground, but had found some habitation either in burial caves or in tombs constructed above ground.

senses.def: a friend and coworker of Paul
a small opening (used in the NT only with reference to the so-called ‘eye’ of a needle)
senses.comment: The hole in a needle is variously referred to in different languages, for example, ‘the nostril of the needle,’ ‘the ear of the needle,’ ‘the mouth of the needle,’ and even ‘the anus of the needle.’

senses.def: a degree which exceeds extraordinarily a point on an implied or overt scale of extent
senses.comment: There are obviously a number of problems involved in attempting to render an expression of extraordinary degree, but it is sometimes possible to express such a degree by building up a series of intensive markers. For example, in Ephesians 2:7 one might translate τὸ ὑπερβάλλον πλοῦτος τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ as ‘his very, very great grace,’ and in 2 Corinthians 4:7 one might render ἡ ὑπερβολὴ τῆς δυνάμεως ᾖ τοῦ θεοῦ as ‘God has very, very great power.’ Such expressions, however, may not do full justice to the intensity of degree expressed in ὑπερβάλλω and ὑπερβολή, since in a number of languages the closest equivalent might be something involving figurative meanings. For example, τὸ ὑπερβάλλον πλοῦτος τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ in Ephesians 2:7 might be rendered as ‘he is gracious beyond anything we can imagine,’ and in 2 Corinthians 4:7 ἡ ὑπερβολὴ τῆς δυνάμεως ᾖ τοῦ θεοῦ may be rendered as ‘God has power beyond any words to describe.’|In this expression in Ephesians 2:7, both ὑπερβάλλον and πλοῦτος (78.15) serve as expressions of degree; ὑπερβάλλον indicates an implied comparison, while πλοῦτος suggests not only a high degree of something, but also value.

senses.subdomain: Pattern, Model, Example, and Corresponding Representation
senses.def: a model of behavior as an example to be imitated or to be avoided
affection for one’s fellow believer in Christ
senses.comment: In the NT the terms φιλαδελφία and φιλάδελφος (25.35) have acquired highly specialized meanings which restrict the range of reference to fellow believers. In nonbiblical contexts these terms would refer to affection or love for persons belonging to a so-called ‘in-group,’ but in the NT this in-group is defined in terms of Christian faith.

senses.def: the psychological faculty of thoughtful planning, often with the implication of being wise and provident

senses.subdomain: Land in Contrast With the Sea
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of χεῖλος ‘lip,’ not occurring in the NT, except as a metonymy for speech; see χεῖλος[b] 33.74) the strip of land close to a body of water
senses.comment: In the NT contexts in which παράλιος (1.61), χεῖλος, and αἰγιαλός (1.63) occur, it is possible to say that χεῖλος ‘shore’ probably involves a somewhat narrower strip of land than παράλιος ‘a coastal region,’ but χεῖλος evidently denotes a somewhat wider area than αἰγιαλός ‘beach, shore.’

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of χεῖλος ‘lip,’ not occurring in the NT) to communicate orally
to be adorned with gold objects
glosses: to be covered with gold adornments
senses.comment: In Revelation 17:4 the phrase κεχρυσωμένη χρυσίῳ involves semantic redundany or what one may also speak of as semantic reinforcement.

senses.def: to provide assistance, with emphasis upon the resulting benefit
to be successful in accomplishing some goal, with the implication that such might be useful
